imo-1962-01.title: Set up an equation
imo-1962-01.body:
Write $n=10m+6$, where $m$ has $k$ digits. Moving the $6$ to the front gives $6\cdot10^k+m$, so
$$6\cdot10^k+m=4(10m+6)\iff 39m=6\cdot10^k-24\iff m=\frac{2(10^k-4)}{13}.$$
So we need $10^k\equiv4\pmod{13}$. The powers of $10$ modulo $13$ are
$$10^1\equiv10,\ 10^2\equiv9,\ 10^3\equiv12,\ 10^4\equiv3,\ 10^5\equiv4.$$
The smallest $k$ is $5$, giving $m=\frac{2\cdot 99996}{13}=15384$, which indeed has $5$ digits. Hence $n=153846$.

Check: $4\cdot153846=615384$. ✓

**Answer: $n=153846$.**

imo-1962-01.title: Long multiplication digit by digit
imo-1962-01.body:
Build $n$ from the right. The last digit of $n$ is $6$, and $4n$ is $n$ with the $6$ moved to the front, so the digits of $4n$ are the digits of $n$ shifted one place to the right.
- $4\cdot6=24$: last digit of $4n$ is $4$, so the second-to-last digit of $n$ is $4$ (carry $2$).
- $4\cdot4+2=18$: next digit $8$ (carry $1$).
- $4\cdot8+1=33$: next digit $3$ (carry $3$).
- $4\cdot3+3=15$: next digit $5$ (carry $1$).
- $4\cdot5+1=21$: next digit $1$ (carry $2$).
- $4\cdot1+2=6$, no carry: this is the leading $6$, and we can stop.

So $n=153846$ and $4n=615384$. **Answer: 153846.**

imo-1962-02.title: Monotonicity and the boundary point
imo-1962-02.body:
The roots are defined for $-1\le x\le3$. On this interval $f(x)=\sqrt{3-x}-\sqrt{x+1}$ is strictly decreasing (the first term decreases, the second increases). So the solution set is $[-1,x_0)$, where $x_0$ is the unique solution of $f(x_0)=\frac12$ (note $f(-1)=2>\frac12$ and $f(3)=-2<\frac12$).

**Find $x_0$.** $\sqrt{3-x}=\sqrt{x+1}+\frac12$. Squaring (both sides non-negative):
$$3-x=x+1+\sqrt{x+1}+\frac14\iff\sqrt{x+1}=\frac74-2x,$$
which requires $x\le\frac78$. Squaring again:
$$x+1=\frac{49}{16}-7x+4x^2\iff 64x^2-128x+33=0\iff x=1\pm\frac{\sqrt{31}}{8}$$
(since $\sqrt{128^2-4\cdot64\cdot33}=\sqrt{7936}=16\sqrt{31}$). Only $x_0=1-\frac{\sqrt{31}}8\approx0.304$ satisfies $x\le\frac78$.

**Answer:** $-1\le x<1-\dfrac{\sqrt{31}}{8}$.

imo-1962-03.title: Follow the four quarters of the motion
imo-1962-03.body:
Take edge $1$ and coordinates
$$A=(0,0,1),\ B=(1,0,1),\ C=(1,1,1),\ D=(0,1,1),\quad A'=(0,0,0),\ B'=(1,0,0),\ C'=(1,1,0),\ D'=(0,1,0).$$
Both points cover one edge per unit of time; the motion is periodic with period $4$. Let $Z$ be the midpoint of $XY$.

| time | $X$ | $Y$ | $Z$ |
|---|---|---|---|
| $t\in[0,1]$ | $(t,0,1)$ on $AB$ | $(1,t,0)$ on $B'C'$ | $\big(\frac{1+t}2,\frac t2,\frac12\big)$ |
| $t\in[1,2]$ | $(1,t-1,1)$ on $BC$ | $(1,1,t-1)$ on $C'C$ | $\big(1,\frac t2,\frac t2\big)$ |
| $t\in[2,3]$ | $(3-t,1,1)$ on $CD$ | $(1,3-t,1)$ on $CB$ | $\big(\frac{4-t}2,\frac{4-t}2,1\big)$ |
| $t\in[3,4]$ | $(0,4-t,1)$ on $DA$ | $(1,0,4-t)$ on $BB'$ | $\big(\frac12,\frac{4-t}2,\frac{5-t}2\big)$ |

Each formula is linear in $t$, so in each quarter $Z$ runs along a segment:
- from $K=(\frac12,0,\frac12)$ to $L=(1,\frac12,\frac12)$,
- from $L$ to $C=(1,1,1)$,
- from $C$ to $O=(\frac12,\frac12,1)$,
- from $O$ back to $K$.

Here $K$, $L$, $O$ are the centres of the faces $ABB'A'$, $BCC'B'$ and $ABCD$. Now $\overrightarrow{KL}=(\frac12,\frac12,0)=-\overrightarrow{CO}$ and $\overrightarrow{LC}=(0,\frac12,\frac12)=-\overrightarrow{OK}$, so $KLCO$ is a parallelogram (hence planar) with all sides $\frac{\sqrt2}{2}$, i.e. a rhombus. At $K$: $\overrightarrow{KL}\cdot\overrightarrow{KO}=(\frac12,\frac12,0)\cdot(0,\frac12,\frac12)=\frac14$, so $\cos\angle K=\frac{1/4}{1/2}=\frac12$ and $\angle K=60^\circ$ (and $\angle C=60^\circ$, $\angle L=\angle O=120^\circ$).

**Answer:** the locus is the perimeter of the rhombus $KLCO$ (a rhombus made of two equilateral triangles $KLO$ and $LCO$ with side $\frac{\sqrt2}2$), traced in the order $K\to L\to C\to O\to K$. To draw it: mark the centres of the front face $ABB'A'$, the right face $BCC'B'$ and the top face $ABCD$, and join them with $C$ as above. ∎

imo-1962-04.title: Reduce to a product
imo-1962-04.body:
Using $\cos^2\theta=\frac{1+\cos2\theta}{2}$, the equation becomes
$$\frac{3+\cos2x+\cos4x+\cos6x}{2}=1\iff \cos2x+\cos6x+(1+\cos4x)=0.$$
Now $\cos2x+\cos6x=2\cos4x\cos2x$ and $1+\cos4x=2\cos^22x$, so
$$2\cos2x(\cos4x+\cos2x)=0\iff 2\cos2x\cdot2\cos3x\cos x=0.$$
Hence $\cos x=0$, $\cos2x=0$ or $\cos3x=0$:
$$x=\frac\pi2+k\pi,\qquad x=\frac\pi4+\frac{k\pi}{2},\qquad x=\frac\pi6+\frac{k\pi}{3}\qquad(k\in\mathbb Z).$$
The first family is contained in the third ($\frac\pi6+\frac\pi3=\frac\pi2$, step $\pi=3\cdot\frac\pi3$).

**Answer:** $x=\dfrac\pi4+\dfrac{k\pi}2$ or $x=\dfrac\pi6+\dfrac{k\pi}3$, $k\in\mathbb Z$. (Check $x=\frac\pi2$: $0+1+0=1$ ✓.)

imo-1962-05.title: Reduce to a triangle with known base, angle and difference of sides
imo-1962-05.body:
We construct a convex quadrilateral $ABCD$, i.e. $D$ on the arc $AC$ of $K$ not containing $B$ (the other two arcs are handled in the same way, with the roles of $A,B,C$ permuted). By Pitot's theorem and its converse, a convex quadrilateral has an incircle iff $AB+CD=BC+DA$. Relabelling $A\leftrightarrow C$ if necessary, assume $BC\ge AB$ and set $\delta=BC-AB\ge0$. We need
$$DC-DA=\delta.$$
If $\delta=0$, take $D$ the midpoint of arc $AC$ (then $DA=DC$ and $ABCD$ is a kite). Let $\delta>0$ and write $\beta=\angle ABC$.

**Analysis.** Since $ABCD$ is cyclic, $\angle ADC=180^\circ-\beta$. Let $E$ be the point of segment $DC$ with $DE=DA$ (possible as $DC>DA$). Then $EC=DC-DA=\delta$, and in the isosceles triangle $ADE$ the base angles are $\frac{180^\circ-\angle ADC}{2}=\frac\beta2$, so
$$\angle AEC=180^\circ-\frac\beta2.$$

**Construction.**
1. Construct $BC-AB=\delta$ and the angle $180^\circ-\frac\beta2$ (bisect $\beta$).
2. On the side of line $AC$ opposite to $B$, draw the arc $\gamma$ of points $X$ with $\angle AXC=180^\circ-\frac\beta2$.
3. Let $E$ be the intersection of $\gamma$ with the circle with centre $C$ and radius $\delta$.
4. Let $D$ be the second intersection of the ray $CE$ with $K$.

**Proof.** Points on the far side of $AC$ that see $AC$ under the angle $180^\circ-\beta$ form the arc of $K$; points seeing it under the larger angle $180^\circ-\frac\beta2$ lie inside $K$. So $E$ is inside $K$, and $D$ lies beyond $E$ on ray $CE$, on arc $AC$ not containing $B$. Then $\angle ADE=\angle ADC=180^\circ-\beta$ and $\angle AED=180^\circ-\angle AEC=\frac\beta2$, so $\angle DAE=\frac\beta2=\angle AED$ and $DA=DE$. Thus $DC-DA=DC-DE=EC=\delta$, i.e. $AB+CD=BC+DA$, and $ABCD$ (convex, as it is inscribed with vertices in this order) has an incircle.

**Existence and uniqueness.** By the triangle inequality $0<\delta=BC-AB<AC$. On the arc $\gamma$ (less than a semicircle, since its inscribed angle is obtuse), the distance from the endpoint $C$ increases continuously and strictly from $0$ to $AC$; so exactly one point $E$ has $CE=\delta$. Hence for each of the three arcs determined by $A,B,C$ there is exactly one point $D$. ∎

imo-1962-06.title: Power of the incentre
imo-1962-06.body:
We prove the formula for every triangle $ABC$ (in particular for isosceles ones). Let $O$ and $I$ be the circumcentre and incentre, $\Omega$ the circumcircle, and let the line $AI$ (the bisector of angle $A$) meet $\Omega$ again at $P$, the midpoint of arc $BC$ not containing $A$. Write $A,B$ also for the angles at these vertices.

**Step 1: $PB=PI$.** Since $\angle PBC=\angle PAC=\frac A2$ (same arc $PC$),
$$\angle PBI=\angle PBC+\angle CBI=\frac A2+\frac B2.$$
The angle $\angle PIB$ is an exterior angle of triangle $ABI$, so $\angle PIB=\angle IAB+\angle IBA=\frac A2+\frac B2$. Hence triangle $PBI$ is isosceles and $PI=PB$.

**Step 2: lengths.** The chord $PB$ subtends the inscribed angle $\angle PAB=\frac A2$, so $PB=2r\sin\frac A2$. The incircle touches $AB$ at a point $F$ with $IF=\rho$ and $\angle IAF=\frac A2$, so $AI=\frac{\rho}{\sin\frac A2}$. Therefore
$$AI\cdot IP=\frac{\rho}{\sin\frac A2}\cdot2r\sin\frac A2=2r\rho.$$

**Step 3: power of a point.** $I$ is inside $\Omega$ and the chord $AP$ passes through $I$, so by the power of the point $I$,
$$AI\cdot IP=r^2-OI^2=r^2-d^2.$$
Comparing, $r^2-d^2=2r\rho$, i.e. $d^2=r(r-2\rho)$, and $d=\sqrt{r(r-2\rho)}$. ∎

*(For an isosceles triangle with apex $A$, the points $A,I,O,P$ all lie on the axis of symmetry and $P$ is the point of $\Omega$ diametrically opposite $A$; the proof above applies verbatim.)*

imo-1962-06.title: Direct computation for the isosceles triangle
imo-1962-06.body:
Let $AB=AC$, put $\alpha=\frac A2$, and let $M$ be the midpoint of $BC$; $O$ and $I$ lie on $AM$. Then $AO=r$ and $AI=\frac{\rho}{\sin\alpha}$, so $d=|AI-r|$ and
$$d^2=r^2-2rAI+AI^2=r^2-2r\rho\iff AI^2=2r(AI-\rho)\iff \rho=2r\sin\alpha(1-\sin\alpha).$$
To verify the last identity: $BM=r\sin A=r\sin2\alpha$ (law of sines, $BC=2r\sin A$), and $\rho=BM\tan\frac B2$ with $\frac B2=45^\circ-\frac\alpha2$. Using $\tan\big(45^\circ-\frac\alpha2\big)=\frac{1-\sin\alpha}{\cos\alpha}$,
$$\rho=2r\sin\alpha\cos\alpha\cdot\frac{1-\sin\alpha}{\cos\alpha}=2r\sin\alpha(1-\sin\alpha).$$
∎

imo-1962-07.title: Tangent lengths and incircles/excircles of the faces
imo-1962-07.body:
Throughout, "tangent to an edge" means tangent to the line of the edge. A sphere is tangent to a line iff the distance from its centre to the line equals its radius.

**Setup.** Let $\Sigma$ be a sphere tangent to the six edge lines. No vertex lies on $\Sigma$: otherwise the three edges through it would all lie in the tangent plane at that vertex, but they are not coplanar. For a vertex $V$ let $t_V>0$ be the length of the tangent segments from $V$ to $\Sigma$ (all tangent segments from a point to a sphere have equal length). If $\Sigma$ touches line $XY$ at $T$, then $XT=t_X$, $YT=t_Y$, so
either $T$ lies inside the segment $XY$ and $XY=t_X+t_Y$ (call the edge *inner*), or $T$ lies outside it and $XY=|t_X-t_Y|$ (call the edge *outer*).

**Faces.** The plane of a face cuts $\Sigma$ in a circle (not a single point, since the three side lines of the face touch $\Sigma$ at three points that cannot coincide), and this circle is tangent to the three side lines of the face. A circle tangent to the three side lines of a triangle is its incircle (all three sides inner) or an excircle (exactly one side inner: the excircle opposite $X$ touches the side opposite $X$ internally and the other two sides on their extensions; moreover its tangent length from $X$ is the semiperimeter, the largest of the three). So **every face has $0$ or $2$ outer edges**.

**Which sets of outer edges are possible?** Let $\mathcal O$ be the set of outer edges.
- $|\mathcal O|=1$: a face containing that edge has exactly one outer edge. Impossible.
- $|\mathcal O|=2$: two opposite edges — every face contains exactly one of them; two edges $XY,XZ$ with a common vertex — the face $XYW$ (with $W$ the fourth vertex) contains only $XY$. Impossible.
- $|\mathcal O|=3$: the three edges of a face — that face has three; a path $XY,YZ,ZW$ — the face $XZW$ contains only $ZW$. Impossible. Three edges through one vertex $V$ (a *star at $V$*): the face opposite $V$ has none, the others have two. Allowed.
- $|\mathcal O|=4$: if the two inner edges are $XY,XZ$ (adjacent), the face $XYZ$ has only $YZ$ outer — impossible. If the two inner edges are opposite, $\mathcal O$ is a $4$-cycle (see below).
- $|\mathcal O|\ge5$: a face avoiding the (at most one) inner edge has three outer edges. Impossible.
- Four edges forming a $4$-cycle, e.g. $\mathcal O=\{SA,AB,BC,CS\}$ (inner: $SB$, $AC$): each face has two. But then in face $SAB$ only $SB$ is inner, so the circle is the excircle opposite $A$ and $t_A>t_B$; in face $ABC$ only $AC$ is inner, so it is the excircle opposite $B$ and $t_B>t_A$. Contradiction. The other two $4$-cycles are excluded the same way.

So $\mathcal O=\emptyset$ or $\mathcal O$ is a star at one of the four vertices: **five possible types**.

**Each type is realised by at most one sphere.** For $\mathcal O=\emptyset$, face $ABC$ gives the incircle, so $t_A,t_B,t_C$ are the incircle tangent lengths of $ABC$, and $t_S=SA-t_A$. For the star at $S$: again $t_A,t_B,t_C$ are the incircle tangent lengths of $ABC$, and in face $SAB$ the circle is the excircle opposite $S$, so $t_S>t_A$ and $t_S=t_A+SA$. In both cases all $t_V$, hence all six points of tangency, are determined. The centre of $\Sigma$ lies on the planes through the tangency points on $SA$, $SB$, $SC$ perpendicular to these lines; as the three directions are not coplanar these planes meet in one point. So the centre, and the radius, are determined. (Same for the other stars.)

**(a)** Five spheres exist, so all five types occur. Let $u_V$ be the tangent lengths of the sphere with $\mathcal O=\emptyset$: $XY=u_X+u_Y$ for all six edges. For the sphere of the star at $S$ we saw $t_A=u_A$, $t_B=u_B$, $t_C=u_C$ (both are the incircle tangent lengths of $ABC$) and
$$t_S=u_A+SA=u_B+SB=u_C+SC.$$
Substituting $SA=u_S+u_A$ etc. gives $2u_A+u_S=2u_B+u_S=2u_C+u_S$, so $u_A=u_B=u_C$. The star at $A$ similarly gives $u_S=u_B=u_C$. Hence all four $u_V$ are equal to some $u$, every edge equals $2u$, and $SABC$ is regular.

**(b)** Let $SABC$ be regular with edge $1$. Its symmetry group fixes the centroid $O$ and acts transitively on the edges, so $O$ is equidistant from the six edge lines; the sphere with centre $O$ and radius this distance (namely $\frac{\sqrt2}{4}$) is tangent to all six.

For the vertex $S$, use coordinates with $G$ (centroid of $ABC$) at the origin, plane $ABC$ as $z=0$ and $S=(0,0,h)$, $h=\sqrt{2/3}$; $A$ is at distance $\frac1{\sqrt3}$ from $G$. A point $X=(0,0,z)$ on the axis is, by the $120^\circ$ rotational symmetry, equidistant from $AB,BC,CA$ (distance $\sqrt{\frac1{12}+z^2}$, as the inradius of $ABC$ is $\frac{1}{2\sqrt3}$) and equidistant from $SA,SB,SC$. In the plane through the axis and $A$, the line $SA$ is $\sqrt3\rho+\frac zh=1$, so $X$ has distance $\frac{|z-h|}{\sqrt3}$ from it. Setting the distances equal:
$$\frac{(z-h)^2}{3}=\frac1{12}+z^2\iff 2z^2+2hz-\frac5{12}=0\iff z=\frac{\sqrt6}{12}\ \text{ or }\ z=-\frac{5\sqrt6}{12}.$$
The first root is $O$; the second gives a point $X_S$ below the face $ABC$, at distance $\frac{3\sqrt2}{4}$ from all six edge lines, so the sphere with centre $X_S$ and radius $\frac{3\sqrt2}{4}$ is tangent to all six. By symmetry we get such a sphere for each of the four vertices; their centres are distinct (they lie on different altitudes, outside the tetrahedron). Together with the sphere at $O$ these are five spheres. ∎
